Here's the post, written out in full and in your voice — all your details are in it, the hard parts included. It's ready to paste straight into the blog.

---

# The House at Glenmore, and the 15th of January

I've started this four times. First I thought I'd write it the night I agreed the sale and post it there and then. Then I thought I'd write it after the roof survey, which was the point where the whole thing stopped being an idea. Then I waited for the fall and the leaves and I decided December would be a good month to say it. I know how I sound. Every one of those reasons was a reason to wait and not a reason to say it.

So here it is, all in one place, and it won't need saying again.

**We have sold the house at Glenmore. The sale completes on the 15th of January 2027.** Please put that date in your diaries now so that nobody has to hear it from somebody else, the way most of you heard it.

It's a strange thing to write. I've been part of this family since before some of you were born, and I have never once had to put something like this in writing, so I'm going to do it the way I would explain something to a room full of children who have all come back from playing and want to know what's happening: plainly, in order, and without pretending it's not difficult.

## The house

The house at Glenmore was built in 1931 by Tom's grandfather Pádraig Mulkerrin, and everything about it is of its time. Low walls round the front, the gate with the sign, the haggard behind where the cattle were, the lane going down to the lake, the back step that everyone in this family has slipped on at some stage or other. There isn't a beautiful thing about it and it isn't going to win a prize. But if you stand in the kitchen in the evening with the door open and the wind coming off the hill, you understand why Pádraig built it there and why nobody in this family has ever wanted to live anywhere else.

Tom proposed to me in that haggard in 1979. In the rain. The cattle watched the whole thing and were not impressed. He had been at thepub, allegedly, and he was soaked through and serious about it, and I said yes before he'd finished the question, and he said "right" and went off to tell my mother. That is the version with the romance in it. The version without the romance in it is that he had been at the pub. He was a good man and a great talker and he was a bit of a show-off, and he was my best friend for fifty-odd years, and I miss him every single day and that is not going to stop just because we have sold the house.

Some of you learned to swim in the lake below the house. I know all of you did, in your different summers. Declan in particular would not come out of the water until his lips were blue and his teeth were chattering and I would be standing on the bank shouting at him to get in, and Tom would say, "Leave him. He'll do it when he's cold enough." He did do it. He did it every single day of that summer and by the end of it he was a better swimmer than any of us.

## What's happening

We agreed the sale on the 3rd of November, with Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin's from Maam Cross, they have two small children, and they want to live in the house. They want to live in it. Not let it, not have it as a second place, not put it on a website with a piano in the front room — live in it, with their children, in the way we did.

There was a lot of interest in the summer, most of it from Dublin. That crowd wanted the house as an investment and they wanted it done up and they wanted the bones of it changed, and they were pushing the price up past what the house is honestly worth to a family who wants to put children in it. The price we agreed was fair, and I took the lower one on purpose. I'll not put the figure on here; that's between us and the buyers. But I will say this: I would rather sell the house to the Joyces for a fair price than to somebody in Dublin for more money and a different future for it. That was a decision I made and I would make it again.

There's a survey from September, from Ó Flaithearta's, and there is a number in my head now and the number is thirty-eight thousand. Thirty-eight thousand for the slates and the back chimney, plus the damp in the back bedroom, which has been getting worse for years and which I have been quietly hoping would sort itself out, as damp does. The septic tank has to be replaced before it can be sold to anybody, which is the law and would be true whoever bought it. So the money went where the money had to go.

And then there's the fortnightly drive. Forty minutes each way, out and back, since Tom died in March 2024. Open the doors, let the air through, run the taps so the pipes don't freeze, have a look round, drive home again. The house has been empty and cold and it has been perfectly well kept, and it has also been the loneliest thing I have ever done with my time. Some of the family asked me why I kept going out. I don't have a good answer except that it was the last routine that had Tom in it.

## Why

I'm 71. I was a primary school teacher for a career and I'm retired now and I have the bit of me that was always tidying up after other people's children very happy to tidy up after my own house. But I can't go on maintaining it, and I want to be honest about that rather than say it in a way that sounds noble.

In February I slipped on the back step in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up. Twenty minutes. The house was empty, I was on my own, and there was nobody to shout for, and when I did eventually get up I sat on the step and thought: there is nobody here. And I didn't tell anybody. Not one person, not until now.

I've thought about that a lot these last few months, because that is the same mistake, isn't it. Not telling people things. Telling the family about the sale by letting it come out sideways, letting Gráinne hear it and put it on a WhatsApp group, and having my son ring me at two in the morning his time to ask me what was going on. I told him I was selling his father. He said things back that I shouldn't have said, and I've been angry with myself about that, but I wasn't wrong about the sale and I'm not going to stand here and pretend I was wrong about the sale.

And I have been afraid of the house since the fall. Genuinely afraid of it. Not of anything in it — of the quiet in it, of being the only person in a house with four bedrooms and a fire that doesn't light first time and forty minutes of road in each direction. Tom used to say the house should have children in it and not be a museum, and he said it a hundred times, and he was talking about the house but he was also talking about me. He would not have wanted me rattling around in it on my own at 71, keeping the rooms aired for nobody.

Over the best part of two years I've come to a conclusion that I don't think I could have come to any quicker. I can keep Tom. That's the thing I actually needed to learn. I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I can keep the fiddle and the photographs and the lamp and the sign on the gate, and I can have my grandchildren and my nieces and my nephews in the kitchen in Oughterard on a Sunday, and the house at Glenmore can be somebody else's beginning instead of my holding on.

Declan was going to come home in the summer. I could have waited until the summer and told him face to face with the house in front of us both and let him take his time. I didn't wait, and I wouldn't have waited, and I'd rather say that straight out than have everybody think I made a decision in a hurry or in the dark. The sale was agreed and the buyers were sensible people and there was a clock running on it, and the truth is I knew that if I waited for the summer I would find a reason to wait a bit longer, and then the year after that. So I did it now. If you're hurt about that, I understand. I'm sorry about the how. I am not sorry about the what.

## What stays

I want you all to know this properly, because "we're selling the house" sounds like everything goes, and it doesn't.

The dresser goes to Úna's. It's the big one, the one with the drawers that don't run properly and the bit of scorch on the top where somebody set a hot dish down without a mat. It was Pádraig's. Úna has wanted it for years and she can have it.

Pádraig's fiddle stays with us, and I'll be having it played, because a fiddle in a case in a cupboard is a sad thing and Pádraig would have thought it was a scandal.

The photographs stay. All of them, the albums and the loose ones and the ones in the biscuit tins. Some of you will be asked for photographs too, so that we can put them in order, so please send them to me rather than to a website.

The Sacred Heart lamp stays. It has been on that landing since before I came into this family and it is going to stay lit.

And the gate sign stays. The Joyces have already said they will put it back up exactly as it is.

And this is the bit I want you to hear: Aoife and Kevin have said that family can come out and walk the land any time. Not "sometime, in theory, we'd love you to" — any time. The haggard, the lane, the lake, the trees. If you want to go up and stand where you stood when you were nine, you're to go up. Just ring them first so nobody arrives with a viewing on.

## Sunday the 13th of December

Before the house is cleared, we're going to have a day out at Glenmore. **Sunday the 13th of December.** Anyone who can get there, come.

Soup and sandwiches in the house, and there's tea, and there'll be more than enough for everybody. Bring wellies. Wear something you don't mind getting the muck on, because it's December and the ground will be soft and we all know what this family's idea of a walk is like.

If you're in Boston or Perth or Leeds and you can't make it in person, that's all right too. Ring me. We'll put the phone on the kitchen table and hold it up to the window so you can see the haggard and the lake and tell us what it's like out where you are. We'll do that.

## To Declan

Declan reads these, so I'll say it directly.

I'm not angry with you. Not one bit of it, and I'm not going to hold it over you, and if I've said something sharp in the last few months I'm sorry for that as well. You rang me at two in the morning your time and I know what that must have been like, and you were right to be angry. I'd have been angry. But the door is open. It has been open the whole time, even when I was saying things I shouldn't have, because I'd rather have this out in the open than have the three of us being careful with each other.

You were eight years old and terrified of the water and you swam every day of that summer because your father told you to leave you alone until you were cold enough. You were right about him. He was a good man and the house was his, and I know what it feels like to be told your father's being sold off. I'd have felt the same.

I'm not taking the house away from you. I'm giving it to two children who are the same age you were at that lake, and there's a bit of that in it, and I hope one day when they're older you'll understand what that means.

Come home in the summer if you want to. Come in the summer, come in the spring, come on the 13th of December. Bring the children. The soup is on.

## The date, one more time

**The sale completes on the 15th of January 2027.**

If somebody rings you about this, or sends you something on a WhatsApp, or tells you a version of it that isn't the version above, ring me and I'll tell you again. I'd rather you had it from me and from Úna and from here, in one go, in the right order, with all of it in, the way I should have done it at the start.

Tom would have said you'd all know the house by now. He would have said it should have children in it. So let's leave it with the Joyces and their two, and let's go up on the 13th and stand in the haggard where he asked me the question, in the rain, with the cattle watching.

It closes on the 15th of January. Everything else after that is just us.

---

*Úna — thank you for keeping this going all these years so there's somewhere to put the truth when it's needed. Right, more of us than we thought for the sandwiches. I'll do a list.*

reasons: Facts fail: the piece reverses the 2am call, saying she told Declan she was selling his father and that he said things back, when Declan said 'selling Dad' and she said things back; it also calls Declan 'terrified of the water' although he refused to leave the lake.
